## Problem

Give a Hilbert space which is not separable.

## Solution

Consider the Hilbert space

$$
\ell^2(\mathbb R)
=
\left\{
x=(x_i)_{i\in\mathbb R}:
\sum_{i\in\mathbb R}|x_i|^2<\infty
\right\},
$$

with inner product

$$
\langle x,y\rangle
=
\sum_{i\in\mathbb R}x_i\overline{y_i}.
$$

It is a standard fact that $\ell^2(\mathbb R)$ is a Hilbert space.

For each $i\in\mathbb R$, define $e_i$ by

$$
e_i(j)=\delta_{ij}.
$$

Then

$$
\{e_i:i\in\mathbb R\}
$$

is an uncountable orthonormal family. In particular, for $i\neq j$,

$$
\|e_i-e_j\|=\sqrt2.
$$

Suppose that $\ell^2(\mathbb R)$ were separable. Then there would exist a countable dense subset $D$.

For each $i\in\mathbb R$, by density of $D$, choose $d_i\in D$ such that

$$
\|e_i-d_i\|<\frac12.
$$

We claim that the points $d_i$ are all distinct. Indeed, if $d_i=d_j=d$ for some $i\neq j$, then

$$
\|e_i-e_j\|
\le
\|e_i-d\|+\|d-e_j\|
<1,
$$

which contradicts

$$
\|e_i-e_j\|=\sqrt2.
$$

Therefore the map

$$
i\mapsto d_i
$$

is injective from $\mathbb R$ into $D$. Hence

$$
\operatorname{card}(D)\ge \operatorname{card}(\mathbb R),
$$

so $D$ cannot be countable. This is a contradiction.

Therefore $\ell^2(\mathbb R)$ is not separable.
